title: XSS Reflection Scanner
description: A tool that crawls target endpoints for input parameters, injects common XSS payloads (script tags, event handlers, SVG injections), and detects which inputs are reflected in the response without sanitization. Demo server has endpoints that reflect input raw, escape HTML entities, and use CSP headers respectively.
summary: Built an XSS reflection scanner with an Express demo server exposing three endpoints at different security levels (raw, HTML-escaped, CSP-protected). All 16 node:test tests passed, covering true positives, false positives, output format, and edge cases.
concepts_demonstrated: Reflected cross-site scripting (XSS)
HTML entity encoding as XSS mitigation
Content-Security-Policy as secondary defence
XSS payload injection and detection
Severity classification (HIGH vs MEDIUM)

title: Port Scanner with Service Fingerprinting
description: Scans a range of localhost ports, identifies which are open, and attempts to fingerprint the service by analysing banner responses. Demo server opens three ports with different services: HTTP (Express), raw TCP echo, and a fake SMTP relay.
summary: Built a parallel TCP port scanner that fingerprints services via banner analysis (HTTP response headers, SMTP 220 greeting, echo reflection). Demo server exposes HTTP, TCP echo, and fake SMTP on consecutive ports. All 22 node:test tests passed on first run.
concepts_demonstrated: TCP port scanning
Service banner grabbing and fingerprinting
HTTP, SMTP, and echo service identification
Parallel async TCP probing with Promise.all
Information leakage via server banners

title: SQL Injection Detector
description: Sends parameterized and unparameterized queries to endpoints backed by SQLite. Detects error-based, union-based, and boolean-based blind SQLi. Demo server has a login form and search endpoint — one using raw string concatenation, one using parameterized queries.
summary: Built a SQL injection detector with an Express + node:sqlite demo server exposing vulnerable (string-concatenated) and safe (parameterized) login and search endpoints. All 20 node:test tests passed, covering error-based SQLi, authentication bypass, and UNION-based data exfiltration.
concepts_demonstrated: Error-based SQL injection via unbalanced quotes
Authentication bypass with always-true SQL condition
UNION-based SQL injection for data exfiltration
Parameterized queries as the complete mitigation
SQL error information disclosure as a secondary vulnerability

title: Hash Collision Demonstrator
description: Compares MD5, SHA-1, and SHA-256 by hashing large sets of inputs and measuring collision resistance. Demonstrates known MD5 weaknesses. Demo server provides a hash-verification API that the tool tests against.
summary: Built a hash algorithm security scanner with an Express demo server exposing MD5 (vulnerable), SHA-1 (deprecated), and SHA-256 (safe) hash endpoints. The server computes a live birthday-attack collision on a 32-bit MD5 prefix at startup. All 23 node:test tests passed.
concepts_demonstrated: MD5 cryptographic weakness and practical collision attacks
SHA-1 deprecation via the SHAttered attack (2017)
Birthday paradox and its impact on hash collision resistance
SHA-256 as the current minimum secure standard
Algorithm agility and deprecation lifecycle

title: Brute Force Rate Limiter Demo
description: Tests login endpoints for brute force protection. Measures how many attempts before lockout, checks if lockout is IP-based or account-based, tests if rate limits reset properly. Demo server has a login route with configurable rate limiting.
summary: Built a brute force protection demo with an Express server exposing a vulnerable endpoint (no rate limiting) and a protected endpoint (IP-based lockout after 5 consecutive failures with 30-second window). A scanner tool probes both and reports findings as structured JSON. All 20 node:test tests passed on first run.
concepts_demonstrated: Brute force login attacks and credential guessing
IP-based rate limiting and account lockout
Fixed-window lockout with configurable threshold
Retry-After header signalling for 429 responses
True positive detection vs. false positive suppression in security scanners

title: File Entropy Analyzer
description: Calculates Shannon entropy of files to detect packed, encrypted, or compressed content. High entropy suggests obfuscation. Demo server serves files with varying entropy levels. Tool analyzes each and classifies them.
summary: Built a Shannon entropy scanner with an Express demo server serving four files at different entropy levels (0, ~4, ~8, ~8 bits/byte). The tool fetches, analyzes, and classifies each file, flagging the two high-entropy blobs as encrypted_or_packed. All 22 node:test tests passed on the first run.
concepts_demonstrated: Shannon entropy as a randomness metric for byte streams
High entropy (>7.5 b/B) as an indicator of encryption or packing
False-positive suppression: plain text and structured data are not flagged
File content classification: plain_text / natural_language / compressed / encrypted_or_packed
Safe endpoint restricting binary content delivery vs. unrestricted download

title: CSRF Token Validator
description: Tests form endpoints for CSRF protection. Checks for token presence, token rotation on each request, SameSite cookie attributes, and referer header validation. Demo server has a funds transfer form — one protected, one unprotected.
summary: Built a CSRF token validator with an Express demo server exposing a vulnerable funds-transfer endpoint (no token check), a protected endpoint (synchronizer token + single-use rotation), and cookie endpoints with and without SameSite=Strict. All 21 node:test tests passed on the first run.
concepts_demonstrated: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attack mechanism
Synchronizer token pattern as the primary CSRF defence
Single-use token rotation to prevent token replay attacks
SameSite=Strict cookie attribute as a complementary browser-level defence
Session-scoped token isolation (session A tokens cannot be used by session B)

title: AES Encryption Mode Comparison
description: Encrypts identical plaintext with AES in ECB, CBC, CTR, and GCM modes. Visually demonstrates why ECB is insecure (pattern preservation). Demo server has encrypt/decrypt endpoints for each mode.
summary: Built an AES mode comparison tool with an Express demo server exposing ECB (vulnerable), CBC (legacy), CTR (unauthenticated), and GCM (recommended) encrypt endpoints. A scanner detects determinism in ECB, missing auth tags in CBC/CTR, and confirms GCM is clean. All 22 node:test tests passed on the first run.
concepts_demonstrated: ECB mode determinism — identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks, leaking data structure
CBC padding oracle vulnerability — unauthenticated mode susceptible to bit-flipping and padding attacks
CTR mode as unauthenticated encryption — no integrity protection despite a random IV
AES-GCM as authenticated encryption — combines confidentiality and integrity in one pass
IV uniqueness requirements — IV reuse under CTR/GCM enables plaintext XOR recovery

title: Input Sanitization Library
description: A comprehensive input sanitization module that handles HTML escaping, SQL parameterization, path normalization, and command injection prevention. Demo server has endpoints that use the library and endpoints that don't. Tests prove the difference.
summary: Built an input sanitization library with an Express demo server exposing three vulnerable/safe endpoint pairs (HTML escaping, path normalization, command injection). The scanner tool sends attack payloads to all six endpoints and reports findings as structured JSON. All 20 node:test tests passed on the first run.
concepts_demonstrated: HTML entity encoding to prevent cross-site scripting (XSS)
Path normalization using path.resolve + startsWith to prevent directory traversal
Shell metacharacter rejection to prevent command injection
Sanitize-at-output vs sanitize-at-input — applying the right layer for each vector
True positive detection and false positive suppression in a security scanner

title: Log File Anomaly Detector
description: Parses server access logs and detects anomalies: SQL injection attempts in URLs, directory traversal sequences, suspicious scanner user agents, request-rate spikes via sliding-window analysis, and consecutive server error bursts. Demo server pre-seeds logs with all five anomaly types alongside clean baseline traffic.
summary: Built a rule-based log anomaly detector with an Express demo server that seeds realistic access logs containing five injected attack patterns. The tool fetches logs over HTTP, applies five detection rules, and emits structured JSON findings with HIGH/MEDIUM severity ratings. All 23 node:test tests passed on the first run.
concepts_demonstrated: URL-decode-before-match to catch %2e%2e and other encoded traversal evasions
Sliding-window rate analysis to detect brute-force login bursts
Consecutive 5xx error tracking as an error-spike indicator
Known scanner user-agent fingerprinting (sqlmap, Nikto, masscan, WPScan)
True positive vs false positive separation in rule-based detection

title: JWT Vulnerability Scanner
description: Tests JWT tokens for common vulnerabilities: none algorithm acceptance, weak HMAC secrets, algorithm confusion (RS256 to HS256), expired token acceptance, missing claims validation. Demo server has a protected API using JWT auth with intentional flaws.
summary: Built a JWT vulnerability scanner with a FastAPI demo server exposing three attack surfaces: alg=none acceptance, HS256 with a weak crackable secret, and missing expiry validation. The scanner probes all three, cracks the secret via dictionary attack, forges an expired token, and verifies the safe endpoint rejects unsigned tokens. All 27 pytest tests passed on first run after fixing an httpx edge case with trailing-space header values.
concepts_demonstrated: JWT none-algorithm attack — unsigned tokens accepted when alg=none is not explicitly rejected
Weak HS256 secret cracking via offline dictionary attack against the HMAC-SHA256 signature
Expired JWT acceptance — missing exp claim validation allows indefinitely valid stolen tokens
Constant-time comparison (hmac.compare_digest) to prevent timing side-channels in secret cracking detection
Strict algorithm allowlist as the correct mitigation for alg=none and algorithm confusion

title: HTTP Security Header Auditor
description: Scans response headers for security best practices: Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, Content-Security-Policy, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy. Grades the endpoint A–F. Demo server has three routes with different header configurations.
summary: Built an HTTP security header auditor with an Express demo server exposing three endpoints at different security levels (no headers, partial headers, full headers). A weighted scoring system converts the six-header check into an A–F grade; only endpoints below grade A appear in findings. All 27 node:test tests passed on the first run.
concepts_demonstrated: Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) preventing SSL-stripping and HTTP downgrade attacks
Content-Security-Policy as the primary XSS execution control
X-Frame-Options and CSP frame-ancestors blocking clickjacking via iframe embedding
X-Content-Type-Options nosniff preventing MIME-type confusion attacks
Referrer-Policy limiting information leakage in the Referer header
Weighted A–F grading to prioritise remediation by impact

title: Keylogger Detection and Flagging
description: A defensive tool that detects behavioural and artefact-based indicators of keylogger activity. Demo server exposes API endpoints that simulate a process list, a registry key scan, a suspicious file path scan, and a network connection report — some endpoints return clean data, others return data seeded with known keylogger indicators (e.g. suspicious process names like 'hook32.dll', registry autorun keys at HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, files in %TEMP% with keyboard-capture naming patterns, unexpected outbound connections on port 443 to unknown IPs). The detection tool queries all four endpoints, cross-references findings against a rule set, assigns severity (HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW), and outputs a structured JSON threat report. Safe endpoints return only legitimate system artefacts and must not be flagged.
summary: Built a layered keylogger detection tool with a FastAPI demo server exposing eight scan endpoints (four seeded with indicators, four clean baselines). The tool cross-references process names, registry autorun keys, temp-directory files, and network connections against a rule set to produce a structured JSON threat report with HIGH/MEDIUM severity ratings. All 39 pytest tests passed on the first run after a one-line fix for a Python 3.14 subprocess handle-inheritance issue on Windows.
concepts_demonstrated: Behavioural detection: matching running process names against a known-keylogger signature list
Registry persistence via HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run autorun keys
Artefact-based detection: keyboard-capture naming patterns in temp-directory files
Network indicator analysis: unknown IPs and non-standard ports as C2 channel signals
Layered multi-surface detection and severity triage (HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW)

title: DNS Record Analyzer
description: Performs DNS lookups using a mock HTTP API and audits email authentication records: SPF and DMARC. Detects missing SPF records, permissive +all SPF qualifiers, absent DMARC records, and DMARC p=none monitoring-only policies. Demo server exposes four domains at varying security levels alongside clean and misconfigured endpoints.
summary: Built a DNS record analyzer with an Express demo server exposing four mock domains at different email authentication security levels (strict, permissive SPF, no auth, monitoring-only DMARC). The tool queries the server's DNS API, parses SPF and DMARC records from TXT entries, and reports misconfigurations as structured JSON findings. All 20 node:test tests passed on the first run.
concepts_demonstrated: SPF (Sender Policy Framework) — TXT record listing authorised mail servers to prevent domain spoofing
Permissive SPF +all qualifier — nullifies the record by permitting any server to send as the domain
DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting & Conformance) — enforces SPF/DKIM policy at receiving servers
DMARC p=none — monitoring-only mode that collects reports but never quarantines or rejects spoofed mail
Mock DNS API pattern — serving structured DNS record data over HTTP to keep the tool localhost-only

title: Email Header Analyzer
description: Parses raw email headers to trace the delivery path, extract originating IPs, check SPF/DKIM/DMARC alignment, and detect spoofing indicators. Demo server provides sample email headers via API. Tool produces a structured analysis report.
summary: Built an email header analyzer with a FastAPI demo server serving four header samples (clean, spoofed sender, missing auth, DMARC p=none). The tool fetches each sample over HTTP, parses Authentication-Results with Python's email module and regex, and reports SPF failures, email spoofing, DMARC failures, and monitoring-only policies as structured JSON findings. All 21 pytest tests passed on the first run.
concepts_demonstrated: SPF (Sender Policy Framework) — DNS-based authorisation list for mail servers; spf=fail means the envelope sender is not permitted
DMARC alignment — links SPF/DKIM results to the From: domain; p=reject is the only policy that blocks spoofed mail
DMARC p=none — monitoring-only mode that generates reports but delivers every spoofed message unchanged
Email spoofing detection — From domain vs envelope sender mismatch as a phishing indicator
Authentication-Results header parsing — the receiving server's tamper-resistant stamp of SPF/DKIM/DMARC outcome

title: OAuth 2.0 PKCE Flow Analyzer
description: Simulates the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow and demonstrates two critical misconfigurations: missing PKCE code_verifier enforcement (any party that intercepts an authorization code can exchange it for tokens) and unvalidated redirect_uri (authorization codes can be sent to attacker-controlled endpoints). Demo server exposes both a vulnerable and a safe authorization flow. Scanner probes for both issues and reports structured JSON findings.
summary: Built an OAuth 2.0 PKCE vulnerability scanner with an Express demo server exposing vulnerable (no PKCE, any redirect_uri) and safe (PKCE required, allowlisted redirect_uri) authorization flows. The scanner detects missing code_verifier enforcement and open redirect_uri acceptance. All 24 node:test tests passed on the first run.
concepts_demonstrated: PKCE (RFC 7636) — code_verifier and SHA-256 code_challenge bind an authorization code to the legitimate client
Missing PKCE enforcement — token endpoint accepting exchanges without code_verifier makes PKCE voluntary and ineffective
Unvalidated redirect_uri — accepting any URI enables authorization code theft via crafted phishing links
Authorization code single-use enforcement — codes deleted on first exchange to prevent replay attacks
redirect_uri allowlist exact-match validation — the only safe approach per RFC 6749 and OAuth 2.1

title: Timing Attack Demonstrator
description: Shows how naive string comparison for secrets leaks information through response timing. Demo server has two token-check endpoints — one using naive char-by-char comparison with early exit (vulnerable), one using hmac.compare_digest (constant-time, safe). Tool measures timing distributions across prefix-match lengths and reports a Pearson correlation coefficient to quantify the leak.
summary: Built a timing side-channel demonstrator with a FastAPI demo server exposing a vulnerable char-by-char token comparison endpoint (amplified with 5ms per matching character) and a safe hmac.compare_digest endpoint. The scanner probes both, measures Pearson correlation between prefix-match length and latency, and flags the naive endpoint as HIGH severity. All 24 pytest tests passed on the first run.
concepts_demonstrated: Timing side-channel attacks — short-circuit string comparison leaks secret length via response latency
Pearson correlation as a statistical measure of timing oracle strength
hmac.compare_digest for constant-time comparison — always processes every byte regardless of mismatch position
Amplification vs real-world attacks — nanosecond-scale leaks require statistical analysis over thousands of samples
Secret comparison best practices — constant-time functions as the mitigation for token, HMAC, and API key checks

title: Open Redirect Checker
description: Tests URL redirect parameters for open redirect vulnerabilities. Checks if the server validates redirect destinations against a whitelist. Demo server has a /redirect?url= endpoint — one validates, one doesn't.
summary: Built an open redirect vulnerability scanner with an Express demo server exposing three redirect patterns: no validation (vulnerable), substring check (bypassable with trusted domain in query string), and strict allowlist validation (safe). The scanner probes all endpoints with attacker payloads, detects both the unvalidated redirect and the substring-check bypass, and confirms the allowlist endpoint is clean. All 32 node:test tests passed on the first run.
concepts_demonstrated: Open redirect attack — attacker-controlled redirect parameter forwards victims to phishing pages via a trusted domain URL
Substring-based bypass — checking if the URL contains a trusted domain fails when the attacker embeds it in a query string
Allowlist validation — parse the full URL, extract origin (scheme + host + port), compare against a strict list
Relative-path-only login returnTo — rejecting http:// and // prefixes prevents off-domain redirects without an allowlist
Scanner detection via raw 301/302 response — follow-redirect mode masks open redirects; inspect Location header directly

title: SOC Tier 1 Alert Triage Simulator
description: A full-stack SOC Tier 1 training simulator using Elastic Common Schema (ECS) alert format. FastAPI backend generates realistic ECS-formatted security alerts across five categories (brute_force, port_scan, lateral_movement, privilege_escalation, malware_beacon), serves them via REST API, and supports SSE streaming. A self-contained HTML/CSS/JS dashboard displays a live alert feed with triage actions, stats cards, a Canvas severity bar chart, and category breakdown. A CLI pre-triage tool fetches open alerts, deduplicates by source IP + rule, scores false positive likelihood, and recommends escalation actions.
summary: Built a full-stack SOC Tier 1 triage simulator with a FastAPI server generating ECS alerts, a self-contained live HTML dashboard with SSE streaming and Canvas chart, and a CLI pre-triage tool that deduplicates and scores alerts. All 33 pytest tests passed on the first run.
concepts_demonstrated: Elastic Common Schema (ECS) alert format — standard field naming used by Kibana SIEM
SOC Tier 1 triage workflow — Escalate / Investigate / Close as False Positive state transitions
Pre-triage automation — deduplication by (source_ip, rule_name) and false positive scoring
SSE (Server-Sent Events) for real-time alert streaming without WebSockets
Alert fatigue mitigation — frequency-based false positive scoring suppresses scanner noise

title: Directory Traversal Detector
description: Sends path traversal payloads (../, ..%2f, ..%252f) to file-serving endpoints and checks if files outside the intended directory are accessible. Demo server serves static files from a specific directory with one safe and one vulnerable handler.
summary: Built a path traversal scanner with an Express demo server exposing a vulnerable endpoint (path.join with no boundary check) and a safe endpoint (path.resolve + startsWith guard). The scanner probes both with basic and URL-encoded traversal payloads, confirms the unsafe endpoint discloses secret file content, and correctly produces no finding for the safe endpoint. All 20 node:test tests passed on the first run.
concepts_demonstrated: path.join does not enforce directory boundaries — it normalises ../ sequences but never verifies the result stays within the intended base directory
path.resolve + startsWith as the correct mitigation — canonical path is computed first, then checked to be a descendant of the allowed base
URL-encoded traversal (%2F as /) — Express decodes query parameters before they reach the handler, so encoding does not bypass path.resolve-based guards
Secret marker detection — scanning response bodies for a known sentinel to confirm actual file disclosure rather than relying on status codes alone
Least-privilege principle — limiting the server process to read-only access on the public subtree as a complementary OS-layer defence

title: Session Fixation Vulnerability Demo
description: Demonstrates session fixation by showing what happens when session IDs aren't regenerated after login. Demo server has two login flows — one regenerates the session, one doesn't. Tool proves the attack path.
summary: Built a session fixation demonstrator with a FastAPI server exposing a vulnerable login endpoint (no session regeneration) and a safe one (old session invalidated, new ID issued on login). The scanner plants a known session ID, authenticates via the victim's flow, and proves access with the planted ID. All 25 pytest tests passed on the first run.
concepts_demonstrated: Session fixation attack — attacker plants a known session ID before login; if the server does not regenerate it, the attacker gains authenticated access
Session ID regeneration on login — the only complete defence: invalidate the pre-auth session and issue a new one immediately after successful authentication
Old session invalidation — deleting the pre-auth session from the server store prevents replaying the planted ID even if an attacker captures it
SameSite=Strict cookie attribute as a complementary control — limits cross-site delivery of session cookies but does not replace regeneration
Scanner detection method — compare the session cookie before and after login; unchanged ID confirms the vulnerability

title: Student Information Management System
description: A secure full-stack web application for managing student records in a UK educational institution. Backend: Express REST API with JWT authentication, role-based access (admin, teacher, student, parent), and SQLite database via node:sqlite. Features: student enrollment with UK-specific fields (UPN, year group, form group, SEN status, FSM eligibility), profile management, emergency contacts, and GDPR-compliant data handling. Frontend: responsive self-contained SPA dashboard with role-specific views — admin sees all students with search/filter, teachers see their form group, students and parents see only their own records. DevSecOps: all inputs validated with express-validator, parameterised queries throughout, bcrypt password hashing (cost 12), JWT with refresh tokens and server-side revocation, CSRF protection via JWT jti double-submit, rate limiting on auth endpoints, security headers via Helmet, audit log of all data access.
summary: Built a full-stack student information management system with Express, node:sqlite, and a self-contained SPA frontend. Implements JWT auth (access + refresh tokens), four-role RBAC (admin/teacher/student/parent) with row-level data filtering, CSRF protection via JWT jti, Helmet security headers, and input validation. All 36 node:test tests passed on the first run.
concepts_demonstrated: JWT authentication with short-lived access tokens (15 min) and revocable refresh tokens stored in SQLite
CSRF protection via JWT jti double-submit — the token's unique ID serves as the CSRF token echoed in X-CSRF-Token header
Role-based access control with row-level SQL filtering — each role receives a different query, not client-side filtering
Parameterised queries preventing SQL injection — injection strings stored safely or rejected by format validation
bcrypt password hashing at cost factor 12 with constant-time comparison
UK Unique Pupil Number (UPN) format validation as business rule enforcement
SEN status and FSM eligibility as sensitive fields restricted to admin-only writes
Audit log recording every data access with user ID, action, and IP address

title: Subdomain Enumerator
description: Uses wordlist-based enumeration to discover subdomains. Demo server acts as a mock DNS-over-HTTP resolver that responds to known subdomains and returns NXDOMAIN for unknown ones. Tool probes a 60-label wordlist, classifies discovered subdomains by sensitivity (HIGH for management/infrastructure labels, MEDIUM for API gateways, LOW for generic services), and emits structured JSON findings.
summary: Built a wordlist-based subdomain enumerator with a FastAPI mock DNS-over-HTTP resolver exposing 10 configured subdomains (www, mail, api, admin, dev, staging, db, internal, vpn, test) and NXDOMAIN for all others. The tool probes a 60-label wordlist, correctly discovers all 10 subdomains, classifies each by severity, and handles unreachable servers gracefully. All 33 pytest tests passed on the first run.
concepts_demonstrated: Subdomain enumeration as a reconnaissance technique — wordlist probing to map an organisation's external attack surface
DNS-over-HTTP mock resolver — serving structured resolution data over HTTP to keep the tool localhost-only
Severity classification by subdomain name — management panels and dev environments are HIGH, API gateways are MEDIUM, generic services are LOW
NXDOMAIN handling — 404 response means the subdomain does not exist; tool correctly suppresses it from findings
Graceful degradation — ConnectError caught on first probe, enumeration halted, empty findings returned without crashing

title: GP Appointment Booking System
description: A secure full-stack NHS-style GP appointment booking platform. Backend: Express REST API with JWT authentication, role-based access (admin, gp, patient), and SQLite database via node:sqlite. Features: patients browse GPs and available slots, book and cancel appointments with 24-hour cancellation policy, GPs view their daily schedules and add consultation notes, admin manages all appointments and views the audit log. DevSecOps: Helmet security headers, CSRF double-submit cookie protection, express-validator input validation, express-rate-limit on auth (20 req/15 min) and API (100 req/min) routes, parameterised queries throughout, bcrypt password hashing at cost 12, JWT with revocable refresh tokens. UK-specific: NHS number field, GMC number for GPs, NHS-styled frontend.
summary: Built a full-stack GP appointment booking system with Express, node:sqlite, and a self-contained NHS-styled SPA frontend. Implements JWT auth with refresh tokens, three-role RBAC (admin/gp/patient), CSRF double-submit cookie protection, Helmet headers, rate limiting, and input validation. All 31 node:test tests passed on the first run.
concepts_demonstrated: JWT authentication with short-lived access tokens (15 min) and SHA-256 hashed revocable refresh tokens in SQLite
CSRF double-submit cookie pattern — matching X-CSRF-Token header and csrf_token cookie required on all state-changing requests
Role-based access control with ownership checks — patients can only cancel their own appointments, GPs see only their own schedules
Parameterised queries preventing SQL injection — no user input ever touches SQL string construction
bcrypt password hashing at cost factor 12 with constant-time comparison
Helmet security headers — CSP, HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options on every response
Rate limiting on auth (20 req/15 min) and general API (100 req/min) routes
Audit log recording every login, booking, and cancellation with user ID and IP address

title: Parameterized Query vs Raw Query Comparison
description: Side-by-side comparison of parameterized queries and string-concatenated queries against SQLite. Demo server has twin endpoints for each operation — search and login — one using raw f-string concatenation (vulnerable) and one using bound parameters (safe). Tool sends boolean-OR and comment-injection payloads to both sets of endpoints and reports which are exploitable.
summary: Built a SQL injection comparison tool with a FastAPI demo server exposing vulnerable (string-concatenated) and safe (parameterized) search and login endpoints backed by SQLite. The scanner probes both pairs with boolean-OR and comment-injection payloads, confirms the unsafe endpoints are exploitable, and correctly produces no findings for the parameterized endpoints. All 28 pytest tests passed on the first run.
concepts_demonstrated: String concatenation in SQL queries enables injection — user input becomes SQL syntax rather than a literal value
Boolean-OR injection — payload ' OR '1'='1' bypasses WHERE filters by adding an always-true condition
Comment injection auth bypass — admin'-- strips the password check from the query entirely
Parameterized queries as the complete mitigation — the database driver separates code from data at the protocol level
False positive suppression — parameterized endpoints return zero findings under the same payloads

title: Digital Attendance Tracking System
description: A full-stack attendance management system for UK schools and colleges. Backend: Express REST API with SQLite storing attendance records per student per lesson/period. Features: mark attendance (present/late/absent/authorised absence), bulk mark entire classes, view attendance percentage per student, trigger alerts when attendance drops below 90% (UK statutory threshold), generate class reports, audit log of all data access. Frontend: teacher dashboard showing class register with one-click marking, student portal showing own attendance history with percentage. DevSecOps: JWT auth with teacher/admin/student roles, CSRF double-submit cookie protection, Helmet security headers, express-validator input validation, rate limiting on auth and API routes, parameterized queries throughout, bcrypt password hashing.
summary: Built a full-stack UK school attendance tracking system with Express, node:sqlite, and a self-contained SPA frontend. Implements JWT auth (access + refresh tokens), three-role RBAC (admin/teacher/student) with SQL-level row filtering, CSRF double-submit cookie protection, Helmet headers, rate limiting, and express-validator input validation. All 35 node:test tests passed on the first run.
concepts_demonstrated: JWT authentication with short-lived access tokens (15 min) and revocable refresh tokens stored in SQLite
CSRF double-submit cookie pattern — matching X-CSRF-Token header against csrf_token cookie on all state-changing requests
Role-based access control with SQL-level row filtering — teachers see only their own class data, students see only their own records
UK DfE 90% persistent absence threshold enforced server-side with low_attendance flag in attendance summary
Parameterized queries preventing SQL injection — no user input concatenated into SQL strings
bcrypt password hashing at cost factor 12
Helmet security headers — CSP, HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options on every response
Audit log recording every login, attendance mark, and data access with user ID and IP address

title: TLS Certificate Analyzer
description: Fetches X.509 certificates from a demo server over HTTP and flags common PKI security misconfigurations: expired certificates, self-signed issuers, undersized RSA keys (below 2048-bit), and missing Subject Alternative Names. Demo server uses Python's cryptography library to generate four certificates at startup — expired, self-signed (no SAN), weak 1024-bit RSA key, and a correctly configured baseline. The tool parses each PEM with cryptography.x509, runs four checks, and reports structured JSON findings. The valid certificate produces zero findings, confirming false positive suppression.
summary: Built a TLS certificate analyzer with a FastAPI demo server generating four X.509 certificates (expired, self-signed/no-SAN, 1024-bit RSA weak key, and a valid baseline). The tool fetches each PEM over HTTP, parses it with cryptography.x509, and flags EXPIRED_CERTIFICATE (HIGH), SELF_SIGNED_CERTIFICATE (MEDIUM), WEAK_RSA_KEY (HIGH), and MISSING_SUBJECT_ALTERNATIVE_NAME (MEDIUM). All 37 pytest tests passed on the first run.
concepts_demonstrated: X.509 certificate validity periods — not_valid_after as the hard expiry boundary rejected by all TLS clients
Self-signed certificate risk — without a CA chain, a MITM can present their own self-signed cert; clients cannot distinguish legitimate from forged
RSA key size requirements — NIST SP 800-131A deprecated 1024-bit RSA in 2015; 2048 bits is the current minimum for new issuance
Subject Alternative Names (SAN) — RFC 2818 §3.1 requires hostnames in the SAN extension; CN-only matching deprecated in Chrome 58 (2017)
Certificate chain of trust — CA-signed certs link identity to a trusted root; tool distinguishes CA-signed from self-signed by comparing issuer and subject DNs

title: Council Tax Payment Portal
description: A secure full-stack UK council tax management and payment portal. Backend: Express REST API with JWT authentication, role-based access (admin, finance, resident), and SQLite database via node:sqlite. Features: residents link their property by council reference number, view their band-based annual bill, apply for discounts (single person 25%, student 25%, disabled 12%, severe mental impairment 50%), view a 10-instalment payment schedule, and make mock payments via Direct Debit or card. Finance officers view all payments and generate arrears reports. Admins manage property records, approve or reject discount applications, and monitor arrears. DevSecOps: Helmet security headers, CSRF double-submit cookie protection, express-validator input validation (including UK postcode regex), express-rate-limit on auth (20 req/15 min) and general API (100 req/min) routes, parameterized queries throughout, bcrypt password hashing at cost 12, JWT with SHA-256 hashed revocable refresh tokens.
summary: Built a full-stack UK council tax payment portal with Express, node:sqlite, and a self-contained NHS-styled SPA frontend. Implements JWT auth (access + refresh tokens with SHA-256 hashed storage and server-side revocation), three-role RBAC (admin/finance/resident), CSRF double-submit cookie protection, Helmet security headers, rate limiting, express-validator input validation, and UK council tax band calculations with discount stacking. All 33 node:test tests passed on the first run.

CSRF double-submit cookie pattern — UUID token set as a readable cookie on login; every state-changing request must echo it in X-CSRF-Token header
Role-based access control enforced in middleware — resident/admin/finance roles with SQL-level row isolation, not client-side filtering
Parameterized queries preventing SQL injection — no user input concatenated into SQL strings throughout all route handlers
bcrypt password hashing at cost factor 12 with constant-time comparison
UK council tax band (A-H) annual charge calculation with stackable discount types (single person, student, disabled, SMI)

title: HTTP Technology Fingerprinter
description: Identifies web frameworks and platforms from passive HTTP response analysis. Demo server mimics five tech stacks (WordPress, React, Django, Ruby on Rails, Next.js) plus a clean baseline endpoint, each exposing the headers, cookies, and HTML patterns their framework adds by default. The tool fetches /targets to discover probe endpoints, then analyzes Server and X-Powered-By headers, framework-specific cookie names, meta generator tags, and asset path conventions. Each rule requires at least two independent indicators before reporting a finding, preventing false positives from coincidental header matches. Safe baseline endpoint produces zero findings.
summary: Built an HTTP technology fingerprinter with a FastAPI demo server exposing five tech-stack simulations (WordPress, React, Django, Rails, Next.js) and a clean baseline. The tool analyzes response headers, cookies, and HTML patterns against a rule set requiring ≥2 indicators per technology. All 36 pytest tests passed on the first run.
concepts_demonstrated: Server and X-Powered-By headers as primary framework disclosure vectors — Apache, gunicorn, Express, and Next.js announce themselves by default
Framework-specific cookie names — csrftoken (Django), wordpress_logged_in_* (WordPress), _<app>_session (Rails) are hardcoded into the framework
HTML meta generator tag — WordPress embeds its version string in every page until explicitly disabled
Asset path conventions as fingerprints — /wp-content/, /_next/static/, and /static/js/*.chunk.js are deterministic build outputs
Rails diagnostic middleware headers — X-Runtime (response time) and X-Request-Id (UUID) are enabled by default via Rack::Runtime and ActionDispatch::RequestId
Two-indicator minimum to suppress false positives — a single matching header or cookie name is insufficient evidence
Clean baseline validation — the safe endpoint exposes none of the above signals and produces zero findings

title: Grade and Results Portal
description: A secure full-stack results management system for UK schools. Backend: Express REST API managing subjects, assessments, and grades with SQLite via node:sqlite. Features: teachers enter grades for assignments, tests, and exams; system calculates running average and predicted grade; supports UK grading scales (GCSE 9-1 and A-Level A*-U); generates student progress reports with at-risk detection (students more than one grade below their target); tracks grade trajectory with previous_marks audit trail. Frontend: teacher grade entry form with class overview table, student/parent portal showing results table and Canvas bar chart, admin view with subject management. DevSecOps: JWT auth (access + refresh tokens with SHA-256 hashed revocable refresh tokens), four-role RBAC (admin/teacher/student/parent) with SQL-level row isolation, CSRF double-submit cookie protection, Helmet security headers, express-rate-limit on auth (20 req/15 min) and API (100 req/min) routes, express-validator input validation, bcrypt password hashing at cost 12, parameterized queries throughout, audit log of all grade access and changes.
summary: Built a full-stack UK school grade and results portal with Express, node:sqlite, and a self-contained SPA frontend. Implements JWT auth (access + refresh tokens), four-role RBAC (admin/teacher/student/parent) with SQL-level row isolation, CSRF double-submit cookie protection, Helmet security headers, rate limiting, and express-validator input validation. UK grade schemes (GCSE 9-1 and A-Level A*-U) computed server-side from raw marks. All 40 node:test tests passed on the first run after fixing SQLite string literal quoting.
concepts_demonstrated: JWT authentication with short-lived access tokens (15 min) and SHA-256 hashed revocable refresh tokens stored in SQLite
CSRF double-submit cookie pattern — UUID token set as readable cookie on login; every state-changing request must echo it in X-CSRF-Token header and Cookie
Four-role RBAC with SQL-level row isolation — teachers see only their subject data, students see only their own grades, parents see only their linked child's data
UK GCSE 9-1 grading — server-side percentage-to-grade conversion; 85%+ = 9, 75%+ = 8, down to U below 5%
UK A-Level A*-U grading — 90%+ = A*, 80%+ = A, down to U below 40%
At-risk detection — students whose current average falls more than one grade below their target are flagged server-side
Grade audit trail — previous_marks stored on every grade update for full change history
Parameterized queries preventing SQL injection — all node:sqlite operations use prepared statements with bound parameters
bcrypt password hashing at cost factor 12 with constant-time comparison

title: TOTP Multi-Factor Authentication
description: Implements TOTP (RFC 6238) generation and verification. Demo server has a login that requires TOTP after password. Tool generates valid and invalid codes, tests time-window tolerance, and replay protection. Demo server exposes a vulnerable endpoint (±5-minute acceptance window, no replay protection) and a safe endpoint (±30-second window with per-code de-duplication). The scanner probes both, demonstrating that a replayed code and a 3-minute-old code are both accepted by the vulnerable endpoint and rejected by the safe one.
summary: Built a TOTP MFA vulnerability scanner with a FastAPI demo server exposing a vulnerable TOTP endpoint (±5-minute window, no replay protection) and a safe endpoint (±30-second window, code de-duplication). Tool implements the RFC 6238 HOTP/TOTP algorithm from stdlib and probes both endpoints. All 24 pytest tests passed on the first run.
concepts_demonstrated: RFC 6238 TOTP algorithm — HMAC-SHA1 over a time-step counter, dynamic truncation to 6 digits
TOTP replay attack — without per-code de-duplication, a valid code can be submitted multiple times within the 30-second window
Wide time-window acceptance — servers using ±10 steps (±5 minutes) extend the attack window far beyond RFC 6238's ±1-step recommendation
Constant-time code tracking — used codes stored as (username, code) tuples; O(1) lookup prevents replay
TOTP as a shared secret — security depends entirely on the TOTP secret never being disclosed; replay and wide-window flaws both erode the time-limited protection

title: Right to Rent Verification System
description: A secure full-stack UK Right to Rent compliance management system for landlords. Backend: Express REST API with JWT authentication, role-based access (landlord, admin), and SQLite database via node:sqlite. Features: landlords register tenants per property, record which documents were checked (passport, BRP, share code, EEA identity card, ILR, certificate of right of abode), record check date and permission type, system auto-calculates follow-up date as 28 days before permission expiry, alerts for checks expiring within 28 days, generates compliance certificates per tenant confirming right to rent status. DevSecOps: Helmet security headers, CSRF double-submit cookie protection, express-validator input validation (including UK postcode regex), express-rate-limit on auth (20 req/15 min) and API (100 req/min) routes, parameterized queries throughout, bcrypt password hashing at cost 12, JWT with jti-randomised revocable refresh tokens, role-based access control. UK compliance: Immigration Act 2014, Home Office Right to Rent Code of Practice.
summary: Built a full-stack UK Right to Rent compliance system with Express, node:sqlite, and a self-contained NHS-styled SPA frontend. Implements JWT auth (access + refresh tokens with jti-randomised hashes for collision-safe revocation), two-role RBAC (landlord/admin), CSRF double-submit cookie protection, Helmet security headers, rate limiting, and express-validator input validation including UK postcode regex. Follow-up dates auto-computed 28 days before permission expiry. Compliance certificates show live status (compliant/expiring_soon/expired). All 32 node:test tests passed.

Server-side status computation — compliant/expiring_soon/expired derived fresh on each API response, never stored or trusted from client
Parameterized queries preventing SQL injection throughout all route handlers
bcrypt password hashing at cost factor 12 with constant-time comparison
Helmet security headers — CSP, HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options on every response
UK postcode format validation via regex (express-validator) as business rule enforcement
express-rate-limit on auth (20 req/15 min) and API (100 req/min) routes

title: CORS Misconfiguration Scanner
description: Detects dangerous Cross-Origin Resource Sharing policies: wildcard ACAO (any origin can read responses), reflected origin with credentials (server echoes back attacker Origin + ACAC: true, allowing any page to make credentialed cross-origin requests), and null origin with credentials (sandboxed iframes can steal authenticated responses). Demo server exposes three vulnerable endpoints at different CORS misconfiguration levels and one safe strict-allowlist endpoint. Tool probes each with attacker and null origins and reports structured JSON findings with severity ratings.
summary: Built a CORS misconfiguration scanner with a FastAPI demo server exposing three vulnerable CORS policies (wildcard, reflected-origin-with-credentials, null-origin-with-credentials) and one safe strict-allowlist endpoint. The scanner probes each with attacker and null origins, correctly identifies all three misconfigurations, and produces zero findings for the allowlist endpoint. All 33 pytest tests passed on the first run.
concepts_demonstrated: CORS wildcard (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *) — any origin can read the response; harmless for public APIs but dangerous if auth is later added
Reflected origin with credentials — echoing the incoming Origin header verbatim plus ACAC: true allows any attacker page to make credentialed cross-origin requests
Null origin acceptance — sandboxed iframes (data: URIs, srcdoc) send Origin: null; accepting it with credentials permits those contexts to read authenticated responses
Strict allowlist validation — only origins on a pre-approved list receive the ACAO header; the Vary: Origin header is required to prevent CDN caching issues
CORS as a browser control — curl and httpx bypass it freely; authentication must still be enforced server-side regardless of CORS policy

title: Fee and Payment Management System
description: A full-stack school fee management system tailored to UK independent schools and colleges. Backend: Express REST API with JWT authentication, role-based access (admin, finance, parent), and SQLite database via node:sqlite. title: File Integrity Checker
description: Computes SHA-256 hashes of files, stores a baseline, then detects modifications by comparing current hashes against the baseline. Demo server serves a set of files via API — four files remain unchanged (clean) and two have been silently tampered with: auth.py has its password verification replaced with a backdoor that always returns True, and db_connector.py has a reverse-shell subprocess injected alongside the legitimate database code. The tool fetches the integrity manifest from /files (filename + baseline hash), re-hashes each file's current content, and reports mismatches as INTEGRITY_VIOLATION findings.
summary: Built a file integrity monitoring tool with a FastAPI demo server serving six files (four clean, two tampered — a backdoored auth handler and a reverse-shell injected database connector). The tool fetches an integrity manifest, re-hashes current file content, and flags any SHA-256 mismatch as a HIGH-severity INTEGRITY_VIOLATION. All 27 pytest tests passed on the first run.
concepts_demonstrated: SHA-256 as a cryptographic integrity primitive — any byte change produces a completely different hash (avalanche property)
Baseline hash manifest pattern — storing known-good hashes separately from the files being monitored, so tampering is detectable even after the fact
Post-exploitation persistence detection — FIM catches attacker modifications to auth handlers and database connectors that establish backdoors or C2 channels
False positive suppression — unchanged files produce zero findings, confirming the tool only alerts on genuine mismatches
Graceful degradation — unreachable server returns empty findings and a descriptive summary without crashing
